title: Who controls the only way out of the Black Sea?

post.caption: The World's Chokepoints: the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles. Rumeli Hisarı (1452), Russia's way out, the Dardanelles attack of 1915, the Montreux Convention (1936) and Turkey's 2022 closure to warships. Images: public domain (NASA, Royal Navy). Map data: Natural Earth.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: Who controls the only way out of the Black Sea?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Turkey. The Bosphorus and the Dardanelles are the Black Sea's only link to the oceans.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: Where exactly are they?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: The Bosphorus runs right through Istanbul. The Dardanelles lie further south, past the Sea of Marmara.

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: The Bosphorus is about thirty-one kilometres long and, at its narrowest, about seven hundred metres wide.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: Who fought over it first?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Everyone. In 1452, Sultan Mehmed the Second built Rumeli Hisarı, a castle to cut the strait. A year later, Constantinople fell.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: Why did Russia care so much?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Russia's fleet sat in the Black Sea. For centuries it wanted a way out, and Britain and France wanted to keep it in.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: Did anyone try to force the straits?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: In 1915, a British and French fleet attacked the Dardanelles. On the eighteenth of March, mines sank three battleships, and the fleet turned back.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: So who makes the rules today?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: A treaty signed at Montreux in 1936. In peacetime, merchant ships pass freely. Turkey controls the warships.

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Warships from outside the Black Sea are limited in size, and may stay only twenty-one days.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: Has Turkey ever used that power?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: In 2022, after Russia invaded Ukraine, Turkey called it a war and closed the straits to warships of the fighting sides.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: And today?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Tens of thousands of ships pass every year: tankers, grain ships and ferries, right past people's homes.

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: The view has hardly changed in centuries.

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Next time: the Strait of Malacca. Like the video and follow History Sketches.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: And tell us in the comments what you think!
